title: The filter
learned: Subtractive synthesis: start with a bright wave, take away what you do not want
CUTOFF sets where the filter starts to cut; lowpass keeps what is below it
RESONANCE boosts the frequencies right at the cutoff: the filter sings
A module is only heard if its output goes somewhere

steps.why: A sawtooth sounds bright and buzzy because it is full of overtones: quieter, higher tones above the note you hear. Most classic synths make their sound by starting from such a rich wave and taking away what they do not want. That is subtractive synthesis, and the tool for taking away is the filter.
steps.do: You hear a sawtooth: oscillator → amplifier → console → speakers. Next to the oscillator is a filter (JX-FLT), not wired yet. Press Next.

steps.why: The sound has to go through the filter on its way to the amplifier. First the way in.
steps.do: Hold Ctrl and drag a new cable from SAW of the oscillator to IN of the filter (SAW already has a cable: a plain drag would move it).
steps.after: Nothing changed: the filter gets the sawtooth, but its output goes nowhere, so you do not hear it. A module is only heard when its output reaches the speakers.

steps.why: Now the way out: the filtered sound replaces the raw one in the amplifier.
steps.do: Drag a cable from OUT of the filter to IN 1 of the amplifier. IN 1 already has the cable from SAW: the new cable replaces it.
steps.after: The sound is softer and darker: the chain is now oscillator → filter → amplifier. The filter is a lowpass: it lets the low frequencies pass and turns the high ones down.

steps.why: The most important knob of a filter is CUTOFF: the frequency where it starts to cut.
steps.do: Press F1 and turn CUTOFF of the filter slowly all the way down, then up again.
steps.after: Going down, the overtones disappear one after another: the sound gets duller, then only a soft thump of the note is left, then nothing. Going up, it opens again. This sweep is the sound of almost every synth you have heard.

steps.why: RESONANCE feeds part of the output back into the filter, so the frequencies right at the cutoff get louder.
steps.do: Turn RESONANCE past the middle, then sweep CUTOFF again.
steps.after: The filter now sings: a peak whistles along as you move the cutoff, like a vowel 'eeoww'. A little resonance adds character; a lot makes the filter ring on its own.
steps.try: Turn RESONANCE almost fully up and move CUTOFF slowly: the filter whistles its own tone. Turn the level down on the amplifier first: it can get loud.

steps.why: Lowpass is the classic, but a filter can also keep other parts of the sound.
steps.do: Turn the TYPE knob of the filter: its four positions are lowpass, bandpass, highpass and notch (the small pictures around the knob).
steps.after: Highpass keeps the highs and removes the lows: thin. Bandpass keeps only a band around the cutoff: like a telephone. Notch removes just that band: hollow. Each type shapes the same wave into a different colour.
steps.try: Turn TYPE back to the first position (lowpass) before you go on.

steps.do: A rich wave and a filter that takes away: that is subtractive synthesis. Press Next to finish.
